items.t: Volkswagen Loosens Its Zero-Wage Playbook as a 1% Margin Leaves Little Room for Error
sum: Volkswagen has quietly widened the goalposts on its global pay policy. According to a Spiegel report published today, a revised internal document now centres on bringing labour costs down to competitive levels, leaving open the possibility of pay rounds with no increases at all. The shift matters to investors for a single reason: whether Europe's biggest carmaker can squeeze out enough savings to steady a business whose profitability has collapsed.

The original instruction, issued in early October, was considerably blunter. Personnel chiefs worldwide were told to push through collective agreements running to 2030 that avoided salary increases wherever possible, while also trimming bonuses, special payments and allowances. That version reached into both base-pay progression and supplementary compensation. The document drafted roughly three weeks later strikes a different tone, focusing on the competitive cost level that zero rounds might help achieve — and making no reference to variable pay. Volkswagen declined to comment on the change, citing the confidentiality of internal papers.

The world works council welcomed the adjustment, a signal that the softer line may find readier acceptance among employees — provided the newly opened room for manoeuvre is actually used. The commercial test, though, remains the cost relief ultimately delivered. What has changed is the emphasis: from individual pay instruments to a target cost level.

The pressure behind that target is easy to see in the numbers. Volkswagen is guiding toward an operating return on sales of at most 1% for 2026, a fraction of the 4–5.5% it once targeted. Restructuring charges, weakness in China and intensifying competition are all weighing on the business, compounded by US tariffs and soft demand.

The nine-month figures published on 29 October lay out the damage. Revenue came in at EUR 233.4 billion, but operating profit reached just EUR 0.1 billion, dragged down by EUR 8.7 billion in special items. For the full year the group expects turnover of around EUR 315 billion. The Brand Group Core, reporting a day later, saw its nine-month operating result slip to EUR 4.33 billion from EUR 4.72 billion a year earlier, with its return on sales falling to 4.1% from 4.4%.

sum: Continental received original-equipment approval for the new Volkswagen ID. Cross on Thursday, November 5, 2026. The approval gives the tire maker a factory-fit program for Volkswagen's all-electric compact SUV, according to Continental.

The ID. Cross leaves the factory on Continental's EcoContact 7 summer tire in 17-, 18- and 19-inch sizes. Volkswagen recommends the WinterContact TS 870 P for colder months and the 18-inch AllSeasonContact 2 for drivers seeking a year-round tire.

sum: Düsseldorf-based Rheinmetall AG saw its shares plunge more than 17% by 10:00 CET on Thursday after the German defence group cut its annual sales and profit margin forecasts.

In a statement released on Wednesday evening, the company said it now expects revenue of approximately €13.2bn for 2026, down from its previous forecast of €13.7bn–€14.2bn. The operating margin is expected to reach around 18.5%, down from 19%.
The company said a major German military order under the Arminius project was now unlikely to be placed this year, pushing the associated advance payments and revenue into 2027.
Arminius is Germany's planned large-scale purchase of Boxer wheeled armoured vehicles, produced by Rheinmetall and fellow defence group KNDS.
Rheinmetall also expects less revenue than planned from newer activities in its weapons and ammunition business, particularly its cooperation with Dutch company Destinus.
Separately, delays in acceptance checks for batches of artillery ammunition will push some revenue into 2027, it said.

Volkswagen Keeps Deutsche Bank's Buy Rating Despite Trimmed Target as China Slide and Porsche Writed
sum: Deutsche Bank has trimmed its price target on Volkswagen's preference shares from EUR 105 to EUR 100 while leaving its buy recommendation in place, a two-speed signal that separates the bank from JPMorgan's more guarded stance on the embattled automaker.

Analyst Tim Rokossa cut the target following a sit-down with VW finance chief Arno Antlitz, an exchange he described as constructive. Talks centered on the ongoing restructuring, cost reduction in Germany and the worsening situation in China. The lower target nonetheless shows that even a positive read on management's plans was not enough to justify an unchanged valuation. The stock added 0.6% in the prior session.

JPMorgan had already moved on Friday, slashing its target from EUR 110 to EUR 85 after the quarterly figures while reaffirming a neutral rating. Media reports pointed to heavy one-off and write-down effects in the most recent quarter as the trigger. Both houses are marking down their valuation expectations; they part ways on what investors should do about it. A reduced target does not amount to a sell call — Deutsche Bank's underlying view stays positive, whereas JPMorgan remains on the sidelines.

The weaker earnings base explains the caution. Volkswagen booked a net loss after tax of EUR 5.8 billion for the third quarter of 2026, dragged down in large part by a non-cash Porsche goodwill impairment of EUR 6.4 billion. That figure cannot be read simply as a verdict on day-to-day operations — but neither does the write-down excuse the operating problems. Earnings power at the core Volkswagen brand remains the key test of the overhaul.

For the first nine months of 2026, the group reported operating profit of EUR 71 million, down from EUR 5,408 million a year earlier. Before special items, operating profit reached EUR 8.8 billion. Management stressed the immediate need for action in light of the nine-month balance sheet. For the full year, Volkswagen expects revenue of around EUR 315 billion and an operating return on sales of up to 1%.
At the brand level, Volkswagen Pkw generated operating profit of EUR 813 million from January to September 2026, a 1.3% operating margin that leaves limited financial headroom.

items.t: Rivian Stocks Surge 9% With UBS Upgrade Facing an $80 Million Automotive Gap
sum: Rivian RIVN, the electric-vehicle and autonomy developer, climbed 9% to $13.26 at 10:10 a.m. ET on November 2 as UBS upgraded the shares to Buy from Neutral, keeping its $17 target. That gives investors a fresh reason to revisit the company after its recent selloff. The earnings mix still deserves scrutiny: consolidated gross profit is positive, while making vehicles remains a money-losing business.

Rivian's October 29 results put that challenge in numbers. Automotive revenue reached $1.550 billion, producing an $80 million gross loss and an implied gross margin of negative 5.2%. Software and services generated $256 million in gross profit, lifting the consolidated total to $176 million. That segment includes Volkswagen joint-venture development work and repair income, so treating its entire profit as evidence of an autonomy subscription breakthrough would overstate the case.

The GuruFocus snapshot adds a caution flag: Rivian's GF Score of 57 out of 100 combines stronger value and momentum readings with weak profitability and growth readings. The rally may reflect renewed appetite for the opportunity, but sustained progress in vehicle margins remains the key test as R2 scales. December's Autonomy and AI Day could offer another product catalyst; closing the manufacturing profit gap will require evidence from the automotive business itself.

VW's Preferred Shares Caught in the Crossfire as Porsche SE Demands an End to 'Taboos'
sum: The simmering conflict at Volkswagen has escalated into open confrontation, with the company's largest shareholder now publicly demanding that management abandon long-standing taboos around plant closures and job cuts. The Porsche SE holding company, which controls a significant stake in the Wolfsburg-based automaker, has urged the board to seriously consider shuttering facilities to accelerate the pace of restructuring — a move that has dramatically intensified pressure on CEO Oliver Blume's leadership team.

The Porsche SE's intervention comes at a particularly volatile moment. Just days earlier, Volkswagen's supervisory board had rejected the management board's revised austerity package, known as "Group Target Picture 2030," which includes potential plant closures and aims to fundamentally overhaul the company's cost structure. The board's decision to block the plan — at least temporarily — has exposed deep fractures between management and labor representatives, with another supervisory board meeting on the closure plans scheduled for September.

The stakes could hardly be higher. According to a Spiegel report, Volkswagen is considering closing four German plants starting in 2031 — Zwickau and Emden first, followed by Hannover in 2032 and the Audi plant in Neckarsulm in 2034. Manager Magazin has reported that up to 100,000 jobs across the group could be at risk. Works council chief Daniela Cavallo did not mince words in her response to management's approach, telling media that "enough is enough" and that the board's treatment of employees was "beyond disrespectful."

The governance battle unfolds against a backdrop of deteriorating financial performance. Volkswagen reported first-half 2026 earnings per preferred share of EUR 2.56, down sharply from EUR 4.34 in the same period last year. Group deliveries fell 6 percent to 4.1 million vehicles, with Chinese deliveries plunging 37 percent in the second quarter alone. The one bright spot was the Brand Group Core division, which bundles the volume brands: it lifted operating profit 4.5 percent to EUR 3.61 billion, with the operating margin edging up to 4.9 percent.

Volkswagen Dropped From Euro Stoxx 50 Blue-Chip Index Over Growing Restructuring Woes
sum: Volkswagen's preferred shares no longer cleared the required bar, with its stock being under serious pressure for a good while now. Shares had fallen more than three-quarters from their 2021 peak, and are presently trading around a 16-year low. The market cap was roughly 38 billion euros despite group-wide sales of 321.9 billion euros reported for 2025.

This is not Volkswagen's first trip through the revolving door, though. Wolfsburg entered the Euro Stoxx 50 a quarter of a century ago, then disappeared from it between 2010 and 2011 during the fallout from the global financial crisis. 15 years after its return, the seat is gone again.

Volkswagen is playing down the significance of the index change, with the company arguing that index membership does not change its fundamental strength. Volkswagen remains an attractive investment, and its ongoing restructuring efforts should improve financial performance in the medium term.

The biggest headache of them all sits in the company's latest forecast. Last week, the group cut its 2026 outlook after identifying 10 billion euros in special effects. A non-cash impairment tied to Porsche goodwill serves as the largest piece of the pie, estimated at 6 billion euros. Revised planning at Porsche lowered the expectations used to determine the brand's enterprise value.

Automotive net liquidity is estimated at 32 to 34 billion euros. Another 2 billion euros in second-half effects covers additional restructuring costs, the sale of the Osnabruck plant, and non-cash impairments associated with difficulties in the Chinese market. The group further cited an accelerated shift in demand toward battery-electric vehicles, which is most evident at Audi and Volkswagen.

All that sits on top of a restructuring plan that calls for more than 35,000 jobs to be eliminated at German locations by 2030. German production capacity could be reduced by 734,000 vehicles. The agreement could deliver more than 15 billion euros in annual sustainable cost savings over the medium term.
As part of the so-called Future Plan 2030, the group will reduce costs by cutting the model range by up to 50 percent while reducing complexity by 75 percent.

Volkswagen Slashes Full-Year Margin Outlook to Under 1%; Porsche Cuts Another 4,100 Jobs
sum: Europe's largest automaker, Volkswagen Group, slashed its fiscal 2026 earnings outlook for the second time in two months, cutting its full-year operating margin guidance from a previous range of 4.0% to 5.5% to "no more than 1%." For an industrial giant with annual revenue exceeding €300 billion, that figure means the group as a whole is now hovering near the breakeven line.

The immediate trigger for this warning is spelled out in a regulatory filing Volkswagen published on September 18: a goodwill impairment of approximately €6 billion (approximately $6.9 billion) tied to the Porsche brand, combined with roughly €10 billion (approximately $11.5 billion) in total special items, and expectations of "further significant deterioration" in the China market. On the same day the warning was issued, Volkswagen's supervisory board approved cutting another 4,100 jobs at Porsche to close an indirect cost gap of approximately €700 million (approximately $802.9 million).
Volkswagen shares closed down 5.6% on the news, while Porsche shares fell 3.3%. Porsche SE, Volkswagen's largest shareholder, also lowered its own earnings outlook, with its shares dropping 4.9%.

Porsche's job cuts did not begin today. In March, Porsche CEO Oliver Blume announced a first round of layoffs affecting more than 4,000 positions. In July, Porsche announced another roughly 5,000 job cuts in Germany, to be implemented primarily through attrition, partial retirement, and voluntary separation programs, without forced redundancies. Combined with the newly announced 4,100 positions, total job cuts over the past two years amount to roughly 13,000.

In exchange, Porsche agreed to extend employment guarantees at its Zuffenhausen plant and Weissach R&D center through 2035, and committed to investing €2.1 billion (approximately $2.4 billion) at the two sites. Employees also agreed to defer portions of salary increases totaling 3.5% through 2035.
This round of layoffs is directly linked to Porsche's sharply intensifying profit pressure.

European Stocks Post Weekly Decline as Inflation and Rate Fears Mount; Volkswagen Surges on Turnaround Deal
sum: European equities closed out a turbulent week in the red, as escalating Middle East tensions, sticky inflation and the prospect of further monetary tightening overshadowed a late-session rebound led by Volkswagen.

The benchmark Stoxx 600 edged up 0.1 percent on Friday to settle at 649.88 points, but the modest gain was not enough to erase a weekly decline of 0.8 percent. The pan-European index had traded lower for much of the day before corporate headlines and easing oil prices helped it recover into the close.

A surprisingly resilient US non-farm payrolls report shaped Friday's trading, signaling continued stability in the American labor market and reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates later this month. Investors are now looking to next week's US consumer inflation data for a clearer read on the central bank's trajectory.

"Fed chairman Warsh's decision to look past labor-market softness at Jackson Hole and focus on inflation has been vindicated and this report gives the Fed more ammunition to tighten in September," said Eric Merlis, managing director and co-head of global markets at Citizens.

The prospect of higher US rates has added another layer of pressure to global equities just as European economies grapple with sluggish growth and rising energy costs. Brent crude traded around $96 a barrel and was on track for its steepest weekly gain since mid-July, a development that carries outsized weight for a region heavily reliant on energy imports.

Volkswagen jumped 5.9 percent to hit a two-month high, topping Germany's DAX index after the supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker struck a turnaround agreement that averted an escalation with unions and shareholder Lower Saxony. The broader European autos index gained 1.1 percent, lifted by the rally.

The automaker faces pressure from US import tariffs, a stagnant European market and aggressive Chinese rivals that have all hurt its margin and hammered the stock. Despite Friday's gain, its shares are down 22 percent so far this year.

Volkswagen plans to cut 50,000 jobs by 2030, shares gain
sum: Investing.com -- Volkswagen announced Thursday it will cut approximately 50,000 jobs as part of its strategic plan through 2030. The cuts are based on a company-wide survey of future staffing requirements.

The automaker set a financial target of achieving a 9% operating return on sales by 2030, which equals an operating profit of about €31 billion. The company plans to invest €135 billion from 2027 to 2031.
The Supervisory Board asked the Group Executive Board to create a new model for decision-making and group structure at Volkswagen Group.
Volkswagen said competitive production cannot currently be guaranteed for its plants in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover, and Neckarsulm. The company is looking at alternative uses for these facilities.
The company's U.S.-traded ADRs gained over 5.5% following the announcement.

The restructuring comes as Volkswagen grapples with one of the most difficult periods in its recent history. The automaker has lost significant ground in China, once a major engine of its growth, as domestic manufacturers such as BYD have gained share with lower-cost electric vehicles and faster product cycles. Volkswagen lost its position as China's top-selling automaker in 2024 and slipped to third place in 2025.

At home, high labor and manufacturing costs have compounded the pressure as Volkswagen's German factories operate with substantial excess capacity. Management has already proposed cutting production capacity and sharply reducing the number of models it sells, while U.S. tariffs and intensifying competition from Asian automakers have further squeezed profits. CEO Oliver Blume has argued that deeper structural cuts are necessary for Volkswagen to remain globally competitive.

sum: The arithmetic at Volkswagen is becoming brutally simple: sell off enough peripheral assets to fund a core overhaul before the core's own deterioration eats the proceeds. This week offered fresh evidence that the first half of that equation is moving — the second half remains very much in doubt.

The most concrete step came on Monday, when Porsche signed a binding agreement to offload its IT and management consultancy MHP to Tata Consultancy Services. The Ludwigsburg-based unit employs roughly 4,500 people and generated around €743 million in revenue in 2025. That deal follows hard on the heels of mid-August's EU approval for the sale of a 51% stake in the heavy-engine subsidiary Everllence — formerly MAN Energy Solutions — to Bain Capital for €7.4 billion, a transaction expected to close by the end of 2026.

Two further disposals are reportedly in the pipeline. Volkswagen is said to be preparing a sale of its development arm IAV to Accenture, with a deal targeted before year-end; that transaction would be accompanied by a future-oriented collective agreement that could eliminate more than 2,000 of the roughly 5,000 German jobs at the company. Separately, the group is weighing a reduction of its Traton holding from 87.5% to 75% plus one share — a stake currently worth around €16.6 billion — though timing and scale remain unspecified. The common thread: raising capital without surrendering control of the truck maker.

The pressure to monetize assets is not hard to trace. First-half operating profit came in at €5.9 billion, down 11.6% year-on-year (the secondary source puts the decline at 12%, a rounding difference), on revenue of €158.1 billion. The operating margin stood at 3.8%. China deliveries collapsed by 26% in the half, and by 37% in the second quarter alone — a deterioration that looks increasingly structural rather than cyclical, particularly as local rivals like BYD gain ground even in VW's home market.

The guidance cut on July 24 — with 2026 revenue now expected to fall 3% to 0% and deliveries to decline 3% to 7% — was the formal acknowledgment that the old trajectory was gone. Since that warning, the preferred shares have clawed back 4.8%. The stock closed Thursday at €74.88, up 3.6% on the day, though no single catalyst for that jump was identifiable.

South America’s New VW Amarok Ditches Ford Ranger Underpinnings, Gets Rendered Ahead of 2027 Debut
sum: The first generation was a thing between 2010 and 2020, being offered with a gasoline engine and several turbodiesel units. Its successor came out in 2022, and is made in South Africa. This one shares its nuts and bolts with the Ford Ranger and Everest, as well as the Bronco, and just like its predecessor, it is also offered with one gasoline burner, and several diesel mills, depending on where it is sold.

Given that the current Volkswagen Amarok is only four years old, one does not expect the automaker to be preparing an entirely new one. But this is exactly what is happening, albeit with a twist. You see, this one will have very little in common with the Amaroks that came before it, and word on the street is that it will be produced exclusively for South America. Reports indicate that production might take place at the company’s General Pacheco facility in Argentina, which is where the first-generation Amarok is still being put together.

A handful of other markets might also get this model, which is said to have been in the making for a couple of years minimum, and despite that, we still do not know a lot of things about it. In fact, we have to mention what the rumor mill says, and that is that it should be the creation of Volkswagen’s partnership with SAIC. Chances are it could share its nuts and bolts with the Maxus Interstellar X, which is a rugged pickup truck made by SAIC that is also known as the LDV Terron 9.

Care to visually compare the upcoming Volkswagen Amarok for South America with the one sold in markets worldwide that shares its nuts and bolts with the Ford Ranger? Well, the former features a split headlamp design, with the daytime running lights being positioned at the top. These sit right below the hood, and further down, we can see a full-width light bar, interrupted in the middle by the corporate logo. The main clusters are positioned below the light bar, on each side of the quite large grille.

Speaking of the latter, it features a pair of horizontal slats. The lower part of the front bumper is on the chunky side of things, and there is also a splitter-like element attached to it. The hood has a similar style and a clamshell-like design, though it is clearly different.

VW's Layoffs Could Hit 140,000. The Family That Controls the Company Already Wrote Off the Loss and Went Shopping for Drones
sum: Volkswagen wants the headline to be about jobs. On August 24, labor representatives told employees the restructuring could ultimately touch as many as 140,000 positions, well above the roughly 100,000 management has floated so far. That's a gap of 40,000 people, treated in most of the coverage like a rounding error. It isn't. But it also isn't the real story here.
The real story is sitting in a filing from a different company, one that most of the coverage of Volkswagen's crisis never bothers to open.

On August 7, Porsche Automobil Holding SE, the family holding company through which the Porsche and Piech descendants control Volkswagen, reported a group result after tax of minus 2.2 billion euros for the first half of 2026. The cause was a 3.0 billion euro non-cash impairment on the carrying value of its own Volkswagen AG shares, plus a smaller writedown tied to Porsche AG. In plain English, the family that controls Volkswagen just told its own shareholders, in an audited financial statement, that its stake in the company is worth billions less than it was twelve months ago.

That same filing disclosed something almost as an afterthought. While marking down its core holding, Porsche SE spent the first half of the year adding money to Quantum Motion, Quantum Systems, and Waabi, respectively a quantum-computing hardware startup, a drone and quantum-sensing company, and an autonomous-trucking software firm. Earnings from that side portfolio jumped from 29 million euros to 148 million, and its carrying value now tops 630 million euros.
The people with the most detailed, least filtered view into Volkswagen's finances are writing down the car company and building a venture portfolio that has nothing to do with cars, at the same time.

Start with what actually happened, because it matters on its own terms. Union officials broke the potential 140,000 figure into three layers: about 50,000 reductions already agreed in Germany, another 50,000 spread across the rest of Volkswagen's production network, and roughly 40,000 more tied to the possible closure of four German plants: Emden, Hanover, Zwickau, and Audi's Neckarsulm site.

sum: Mercedes-Benz shares rose by more than 5% in Frankfurt on Tuesday morning after the carmaker reported higher second-quarter profit, while warning that continued weakness in China would weigh on full-year car sales.
The company cited "in particular, the negative development of the Chinese market" as it said Mercedes-Benz Cars' unit sales were now expected to be slightly below the previous year's level.

This could translate into a decline of between 2% and 7.5% in full-year car sales, according to the definitions used in the carmaker's 2025 annual report. Reflecting the weaker sales outlook, Mercedes-Benz also expects group revenue to come in slightly below last year's level. It had previously forecast broadly stable car sales and revenue.
Mercedes-Benz announced the revised outlook alongside its second-quarter results on Tuesday.
Mercedes-Benz reported second-quarter operating profit of €1.55 billion, up 22% from €1.27 billion a year earlier. Revenue fell by 3% to €32.1 billion from €33.2 billion.

Former VW Engineers Arrested for Insider Trading Tied To Rivian Deal
sum: Two former Volkswagen Group engineers have been arrested and charged in a federal insider trading scheme. The federal indictment alleges the men used non-public corporate data to buy up massive stock positions in EV startup Rivian Automotive just days before VW announced a massive joint venture.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York unsealed the indictment, naming Michael Stamp, 31, and Marcus Plank, 45, as the primary defendants. Both men were German nationals working in California on a temporary assignment for a Volkswagen technology subsidiary. Through their day-to-day access to proprietary powertrain and electronic systems data, they gained early knowledge of the automotive partnership.

While federal prosecutors routinely track suspicious equity spikes through advanced market surveillance algorithms, the case against Stamp and Plank contains a glaring paper trail of digital evidence. According to investigators, the engineers used their personal and work devices to conduct Google searches that directly pointed to their illegal trading plans and anxiety over getting caught.

Some of the incriminating search queries uncovered by the FBI included searches regarding the impending Volkswagen acquisition, the mechanics of insider trading call options, how the SEC catches insider traders, and whether the FBI can track deleted search history.

Despite their apparent concerns, the pair proceeded with the strategy. Shortly after learning of the partnership discussions, the pair began aggressively purchasing high-leverage short-term call options and standard equity positions in Rivian stock.
When Volkswagen officially made the joint venture public, Rivian shares skyrocketed. The sudden market spike triggered the engineers' option contracts, netting them huge, immediate returns.

Stamp pocketed approximately $250,000 in illegal gains and immediately began transferring the funds to his personal bank accounts, while Plank walked away with at least $50,000 after liquidating his option contracts. Additionally, Plank allegedly tipped off a family member who managed to squeeze out $12,000 from the stock movement.

Volkswagen was supposed to manufacture components for the Iron Dome. A shareholder from Qatar blocked the deal
sum: Recent years have not been kind to the German automotive giant. The difficult and costly transition from internal combustion engines to electric vehicles, combined with growing problems stemming from the mass influx of cheaper Chinese competition into Europe, has forced the group known for Beetles, Golfs, and Passats to seek alternative revenue sources. The global geopolitical situation prompted the Germans to open up to the broadly defined defence industry.

One manifestation of this opening was the collaboration with the Israeli defence company Rafael (Rafael Advanced Defence Systems) announced earlier this year. Joint activities were to be based on the production of components for „Iron Dome” anti-missile systems at the Volkswagen factory in Osnabrück, where car production is scheduled to end this year. The partnership was intended to satisfy both parties – the German side would prevent mass layoffs and the factory’s closure, while the Israeli entity would diversify its production, a move justified by security concerns given the tense situation in the Middle East. Under a letter of intent signed in April, the German automotive company committed not only to producing trucks to transport components of the Israeli system but also, among other things, to the production of power generators.

In July, it turned out that these investments will likely not materialize. This is due to a minority shareholder in Volkswagen—the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA)—which reportedly blocked the cooperation in Osnabrück. The main reason? Qatari policy toward Israel. An additional blocking factor was the labor unions within the company itself, which also protested against producing for an Israeli firm famous for its Trophy APS (Active Protection System) and Spike anti-tank missiles.

Despite the fact that Porsche SE holds more than 50 percent of the company’s shares and QIA is a minority investor (approximately 10 percent), Volkswagen management decided to respect the Qatari blockade. This decision stems not only from financial considerations (fears of losing a shareholder) but also from the aforementioned protests by some employees and local activists who want the factory in the German city to remain focused exclusively on production for the civilian market.
